topProblems: The twist narration muddies its own logic: Poppy audibly says 'Lucas' at 3am, then the narrator insists '3am wasn't a dream about Lucas.' Viewers will re-read that as a contradiction rather than a gut-punch, and the balcony reveal loses its snap.

Matteo is set up as a numbered joke ('lasagne. For eleven.') and then abandoned — the gavel beat gets courtroom gravity but no punchline, and the one man whose name was NOT said at 3am exits the episode unpaid. The carb-language runner sits adjacent to the rating premise instead of inside it.

Poppy — the villa's designated scorer of everyone else — is the only major character who never receives a number. That's the episode's biggest missed joke: the premise's cleanest ironic payoff is left on the table.

Alejandro's arrival is thematically welded to the rating engine at the endcard but causally unconnected to Scene 5's kiss reveal. It reads as a scheduled format beat, not a consequence, which softens the run into the CTA.
Scene 4 is the densest scene and runs eight lines with no engineered silence; the 'four' punchline on Brock's water — the best rating gag in the script — gets cut off instead of held.
concreteFixes: Scene 5, narrator lines 3–4: replace 'It was the balcony she pretended not to see' construction with clarified logic — 'She was dreaming about Lucas.' / (beat) 'She was dreaming about the balcony.' This keeps the reveal and kills the contradiction.

Scene 4, after 'Matteo sets the lasagne down like a gavel': add Élodie, flat, mid-sip — 'The lasagne — a nine.' Then narrator, dry: 'The highest score of the night went to pasta.' This pulls Matteo's carb-language inside the rating engine and pays the gavel.
Scene 3, after Matteo's 'For eleven': change narrator's 'Nobody asked' to 'There are nine of you, Matteo.' (beat) 'Nobody asked.' — makes the number do premise work instead of sitting as flavour.
Scene 4, Brock's 'That was a four': add a two-second hold (SFX drop to room tone) before the cut so the episode's sharpest rating beat lands instead of being buried under the scene transition.

Scene 7, Greta line: change 'You are not on the schedule' follow-up so the arrival is caused — Rohan: 'Someone scored low enough to trigger a replacement.' Now Alejandro walks in as a consequence of the firepit ratings, not a format injection.

Scene 8 endcard: before Alejandro's smolder, cut two seconds to Poppy in the Spill Room — 'I don't do numbers.' — then narrator over Alejandro's exit: 'She gave Lucas a ten in her sleep.' Pays off the only unscored character and hands the CTA a second guess to bait.

None of the three characters appear in the other stills. The Indian boy's saffron/white/green does read; the red-shirted man (Spain?) and the blonde in a black swimsuit with a vague red-yellow stripe do not read as any flag at a glance. visuals.overallNotes: The episode holds together across frames 1-5 (kitchen, poolside, firepit, two-shot, confessional): consistent glossy candy-bright 3D, matching chunky character proportions, and instantly legible flag wardrobes (Union Jack, US stars-and-stripes, Brazil yellow/green, Australia green-and-gold, French Breton/beret). Two frames break the show: the opening bedroom still is far too dark, has multiple missing arms/hands and floating candle glows, and the final still is a completely different painterly, semi-realistic render with an unfamiliar cast and unreadable national wardrobe. Recurring cast-wide problems are hands — nearly every frame has at least one fused, elongated or vanished hand — plus props that don't obey physics (a sausage in a water glass, lanterns hanging from nothing, blank book pages, a featureless phone). Two characters (the bearded man in the plain white shirt, the shirtless man) carry no national branding at all and should be re-costumed. Recommendation: regenerate stills 1 and 7, retouch hands in 2, 3 and 4, and lock the beret badge design for continuity.
